prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

My brother's funeral over, the dark-clothed congregation clots the church doors, a lingering aftermath moving into flat light—the sky low and swollen, a storm siren's long expansive notes, evenly measured, so loud the pauses between ring with aftersound. Used to it, no one here appears alarmed, the church ladies filing into his house bearing heavy covered dishes, the funeral flowers. On the muted television tuned to the weather, a small area of Watch now upgrades to Warning; the words stream across the bottom of the screen calling conditions perfect, this town, this house disappeared beneath the map's isolated lesion, its red edges uneven, stalled. The forecasters rely they say on spotters to confirm what the radar cannot—they call it ground truth; until then no one knows anything for certain beyond this inward watching. The room hums, an airless, crowded hive. Their mouths are full, plates layered—fried chicken, deviled eggs, casseroles, bright congealed salads with fruit suspended inside. All of it dust. I have come here too late, his body gone, already ash. The storm's body could be forming now, tightening from cloud to the gyre that will consume its path, all of it a becoming—spiraling a wall of water, mud, dust, and sand; with dispassion taking up into itself the fence line, a barn—the house beside them spared with the same dispassion. Or this, more likely now: siren silenced, the winds diminishing, the light, afternoon's concession to another dusk—severe, more common truth.

After my brother’s funeral, the mourners in black gather thickly at the church entrance, the residue of the service drifting out into a dull, flattened light. The sky hangs low, distended with weather. A storm siren releases long, widening tones at regular intervals, so loud that even the gaps between them seem to vibrate with what remains. No one local looks frightened; they are accustomed to it. The church women make their way into his house carrying weighty covered dishes and the funeral arrangements.

On the television, its sound turned down and the channel set to the weather, a small patch marked Watch has been changed to Warning. Text runs along the bottom of the screen, announcing that conditions are ideal. This town, this house, vanish beneath a lone blotch on the map, its jagged red borders stalled in place. The meteorologists say they depend on people watching from the ground to verify what radar cannot show. They call this ground truth. Until such confirmation comes, nobody can be sure of anything except this tense, inward waiting.

The room buzzes like a packed, airless hive. People eat with their mouths full, their plates heaped with fried chicken, deviled eggs, casseroles, and glossy molded salads holding pieces of fruit in suspension. Everything is dust. I have arrived too late. His body is no longer here; it has already been reduced to ash.

The storm itself may even now be taking shape, drawing tight from the clouds into the rotating center that will devour whatever lies ahead of it. It is all in the act of becoming: a spiral wall of water, mud, dust, and sand. Without feeling, it may lift a fence line, a barn, into itself, and with that same indifference leave the neighboring house untouched. Or, more likely by now, this is what happens: the siren stops, the wind slackens, the light yields the afternoon to yet another dusk—the harsher, more ordinary truth.
outputs.L3:
By the time the narrator arrives, the funeral is already over. They have come too late to see their brother one last time, too late to stand beside his body or confirm the fact of him with their own eyes. What remains of him has already been reduced to ash, leaving the narrator with an absence that feels both final and unreal.

At the house, mourners begin to gather, bringing with them the subdued conversations and awkward silences that follow a death. Then a storm siren rises outside, cutting through the atmosphere of grief. To the narrator, the sound feels urgent and alarming, a warning that demands attention. But the people who live there seem used to it. They continue moving through the rooms, talking quietly, eating, remembering, and behaving as though the siren is part of the background of local life.

On the television, the weather report grows more serious. What had been a Tornado Watch becomes a Tornado Warning, and the map on the screen places the town—and the house where everyone has gathered—directly inside the threatened area. The danger is no longer distant or hypothetical. It has been narrowed down, named, and drawn around them.

Yet even with radar and forecasts, the situation remains uncertain. The forecasters still rely on “ground truth,” reports from spotters who can say what is actually happening beneath the storm. Radar can suggest rotation, velocity, and risk, but it cannot fully confirm the reality on the ground. Someone has to see the funnel, the debris, the damage, the thing itself.

Caught between grief and danger, the narrator imagines two possible futures for the storm. It may gather itself into a tornado, touch down, and tear through the town with sudden violence. Or it may weaken and pass over them as ordinary severe weather, loud and frightening but ultimately survivable. Like the brother’s death, the storm hovers between what can be predicted and what can only be known after it has happened.
outputs.L4:
After my brother’s funeral, the house filled with the strange weather of visitors.

People moved through the rooms in low voices, carrying paper plates and foil-covered dishes, touching my shoulder as if I were a railing they needed for balance. Someone had set out coffee in the kitchen. Someone had arranged the casseroles according to a private logic of grief: potatoes by the sink, ham on the counter, salads sweating beneath plastic wrap. The funeral flowers leaned in their vases, too fragrant, too alive. Their ribbons still said Brother, Son, Beloved, as if language could hold a body in place.

Outside, the sky had turned the color of old metal.

The television in the den was muted, but the weather map flashed red and orange over the county, a wound spreading across the screen. Every few minutes someone turned up the volume. The meteorologist stood before a radar image, pointing to hooks and cells and rotations that were not yet visible from our windows. His sleeves were rolled up. His voice had the practiced urgency of a man who had learned to speak calmly about catastrophe.

“We have a tornado warning now,” he said. “Not a watch. A warning.”

In the room, this distinction mattered. People who had spent the afternoon saying things like “He’s in a better place” and “At least he didn’t suffer” became suddenly exact. A watch meant conditions were possible. A warning meant something had been seen or indicated. A warning meant take shelter.

But even then, no one knew.

The radar suggested rotation. The sirens began their long mechanical wail from town, rising and falling over the rooftops. Phones buzzed in purses and jacket pockets. The county alert came through in capital letters, advising us to move to an interior room on the lowest floor. Still, everyone drifted first to the windows.

That is what people do. We are told danger is coming, and we look for it.

I stood at the back door and watched the maple trees turn their leaves inside out. The air had gone greenish and still, the way people say it does before a tornado, though I had never trusted that description. So much of weather is rumor until it arrives. So much of death is, too.

All week, I had been waiting for confirmation of one kind or another. The call from the hospital had been clear, but not clear enough. The doctor’s voice, my mother’s face, the folded suit chosen for the casket, the obituary proof sent by email, the receiving line at the funeral home—each thing should have made my brother’s death more real. Instead, each became another report from somewhere I was not. Indicated rotation. Possible touchdown. Seek shelter now.

At the visitation, people told stories about him as if placing sandbags against the fact of his absence. They remembered his laugh, his old truck, the time he fell through the dock at the lake and came up laughing before anyone knew whether to scream. They spoke of him in fragments, and the fragments were true, but none of them added up to the body in the casket or the body no longer in it. I had touched his hand because I thought touch would settle the matter. His fingers were cold and firm and unlike him. Even that was not proof, only evidence.

Now the sirens sounded again.

My aunt began gathering the children toward the hallway. My father, still in his funeral suit, went outside to look at the sky. Someone told him to come back in. Someone else said the worst of it was north of us. The meteorologist interrupted himself, listening to something in his earpiece.

“We’re getting reports of debris,” he said. “Again, this is radar-indicated. We do not yet have ground truth.”

Ground truth.

The phrase entered the room and stayed there.

I knew what he meant. A storm could appear on radar as a signature, a velocity couplet, a tight red-and-green knot suggesting winds moving violently in opposite directions. But until someone saw the funnel, until a trained spotter called it in, until a barn was opened and scattered across a field, until trees were twisted out of the earth, it remained unconfirmed. The atmosphere could threaten. Instruments could infer. Sirens could mourn in advance. But the truth, the real truth, waited on the ground.

My brother, too, had become a question of ground truth.

There were documents, witnesses, official times. There was a death certificate folded in my mother’s purse. There was a grave beneath a tent at the cemetery, green carpeting laid over the raw earth so we would not have to see the hole plainly. There was the minister’s voice, the military stiffness of the funeral director, the soft thud of roses dropped onto the casket. There were all the rituals by which the living are asked to accept what cannot be revised.

And still I kept expecting him.

I expected him to come in through the side door, late and apologetic, shaking rain from his hair. I expected him to make a joke about the sandwiches. I expected him to stand behind me at the sink and reach around for a mug. Grief did not feel like knowing. It felt like waiting for information that never arrived.

The house lights flickered. Conversation stopped.

For one suspended moment, the house seemed to inhale. Then the rain came hard, thrown sideways against the windows. The trees bent in one direction and then another, frantic, obedient to forces we could not see. We moved at last into the hallway and crouched there among shoes, umbrellas, and the smell of wet wool. My mother sat on the floor with her back against the wall, still wearing the black dress she had bought for the funeral. Her hands rested open in her lap, emptied of tissues, flowers, programs, all the small objects grief gives people to hold.

No one spoke of my brother then. No one needed to. The sirens spoke. The wind spoke. The house creaked around us like something old trying to remain upright.

I thought of the cemetery, the tent, the mound of dirt hidden beneath artificial grass. I wondered if the storm was passing over him now. It was an irrational thought, because he was beyond weather, beyond wet or cold or fear. Yet I pictured the rain striking the newly turned earth, the flowers blown from their stands, the temporary marker trembling in the mud. Even after burial, I wanted him protected. Even after death, I wanted there to be something I could do.

The tornado did not hit our house.

Later, we learned that it touched down five miles east, near the highway, where it tore the roof from a machine shed and lifted a grain bin clean off its foundation. It snapped power poles, overturned irrigation equipment, drove splinters of wood into the side of a church. No one died. This was said with relief, almost triumph, as if the storm had made a choice and chosen mercy.

But it had not chosen.

It had followed pressure, heat, wind shear, the invisible mathematics of collision. It had dipped where it dipped. It had risen where it rose. One house lost windows; the next kept its porch swing. One field was scraped raw; another stood untouched, the corn still shining with rain. The news showed aerial footage the next morning, damage paths carved across the land like the work of an enormous, careless finger.

That was the ground truth: not meaning, only aftermath.

After everyone left, the house became too quiet. The casseroles remained. The coffee burned in the pot. Funeral programs lay on the side table, my brother’s face printed above dates that seemed impossible in their completeness. Birth, dash, death. A whole life reduced to a line between two numbers.

I walked from room to room gathering plates and napkins, performing the small domestic rites that follow the larger ones. There is always cleaning after grief. There are always cups to wash, chairs to fold, flowers to throw away once they begin to rot. Loss enters like weather, but it stays like housework. You find it in the refrigerator, in the voicemail, in the jacket still hanging by the door.

Outside, the storm had passed, leaving branches in the yard and a pale, rinsed evening sky. The sirens were silent. The meteorologists had moved on to damage reports, interviews, measurements of wind speed based on what had been destroyed. They could tell the strength of the tornado by the things it had broken. They could classify it only after it was over.

I understood that.

Some truths do not arrive as revelations. They accumulate as wreckage. You know the storm was real when you see the roof in the field. You know death is real when the chair stays empty, when the phone does not ring, when no new story can be added to the old ones. Until then, the mind keeps scanning the horizon, waiting for confirmation, mistaking warning for knowledge.

My brother was gone before I could believe it. The tornado spared us for no reason I could name. Between those facts lay the terrible randomness of being alive: the path that strikes one house and not another, the body that fails while others go on breathing, the warning that comes too late or just in time.

Ground truth, I learned, is not the comfort of certainty. It is what remains after certainty is no longer useful. It is the broken branch in the yard, the fresh grave after rain, the untouched house beside the ruined one. It is the evidence we never wanted and cannot refuse.

Only afterward do we know.

Only afterward do we stand among what is left and call it true.
outputs.L5:
**Used Watch Warning: What to Know Before You Buy**

Buying a used watch can be a smart way to save money or find a rare model, but it also comes with risks. Before purchasing, it is important to check the watch carefully and make sure it is genuine, functional, and fairly priced.

One major warning is the risk of counterfeit watches. Popular brands are often copied, and fake watches can look very convincing. Always ask for proof of authenticity, original papers, receipts, or service records if available. If the deal seems too good to be true, it probably is.

Another thing to consider is the condition of the watch. A used watch may have scratches, worn parts, or hidden mechanical problems. Check whether it keeps accurate time, whether the crown works properly, and whether the strap or bracelet is original. For luxury watches, a professional inspection is highly recommended.

You should also be careful when buying online. Only purchase from trusted sellers or platforms with buyer protection. Read reviews, ask questions, and request clear photos of the watch from different angles.

In short, a used watch can be a great purchase, but caution is necessary. Pay attention to warning signs, verify authenticity, and never rush the decision. A careful buyer is much more likely to enjoy a reliable and valuable timepiece.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a literary flash fiction scene in first person about returning too late for a brother’s funeral in a small Midwestern town while a tornado warning unfolds in the background.
counterfactuals.output:
By the time I got back to Halpern, the funeral was over and the sky had turned the color of old nickels.

The church doors were still open, though, breathing out lilies and floor wax. Programs littered the vestibule in damp little drifts, his name printed in blue script like an invitation to a party I had missed. **Daniel Reese Whitaker. Beloved son, brother, friend.** Born in the year the river came up over Main Street. Dead in the year the co-op burned down.

I stood there with my suitcase in my hand while the tornado siren began its long, wounded note.

Nobody came to greet me. That seemed fair.

In the sanctuary, the pews held the heat of people who’d only just left. I could see where the coffin had been by the flattened places in the carpet and the two stray rose petals near the rail. The photograph of Danny still stood beside the pulpit: him at seventeen, sunburned and grinning, one arm hooked around a fencepost like he’d just roped the whole horizon and was holding it still.

I’d flown from Phoenix to Chicago, then driven six hours through rain the color of dishwater, arguing with myself the whole way. I told myself planes were late, roads were bad, nobody could blame me. Then I remembered my mother’s voice on the phone, small as a moth in a jar.

*He asked for you once.*

The siren rose, fell, rose again.

Outside, the town had emptied itself. The bank sign flashed **TAKE SHELTER** between the time and temperature. Across the street, the barber’s striped pole spun bravely in the green light. A plastic funeral wreath tumbled down the sidewalk, paused at the curb, and then shuddered into the street like it had changed its mind about where grief belonged.

I found my mother in the church basement, sitting at a folding table beneath a map of the Holy Land. The casseroles had been covered in foil. A sheet cake with Danny’s name on it sagged in the middle, untouched except for one corner where someone had taken a polite square.

She looked up at me without surprise. Her black dress made her seem smaller, as if mourning had cinched her in.

“You missed it,” she said.

“I know.”

“They played that song you hated.”

“I don’t hate it.”

“You left the room every time he put it on.”

I set down my suitcase. Overhead, the pipes clicked. Somewhere far above us, wind pressed its palm against the church.

“I tried to get here,” I said, and hated myself for how rehearsed it sounded.

Mother folded a napkin into quarters, then quarters again. “He knew that about you.”

“What?”

“That you always tried. After.”

After. In our family, whole decades lived behind that word.

After Dad died. After I left. After Danny stayed. After he put my name on the farm paperwork and forged my signature so the bank wouldn’t take the north field. After I called him a thief. After he said, “Come home and say it to my face,” and I didn’t.

The lights blinked once.

From the stairwell came the hollow thunder of someone descending fast. Pastor Lyle appeared, tie loosened, hair lifted in gray wisps. “Basement’s the place to be,” he said, then saw me and stopped. His eyes did the small-town math: the prodigal brother, late enough to be useless.

“Good you made it,” he said, because he was paid to believe in mercy.

The radio on the counter crackled to life. A voice, calm and official, named counties like a prayer list. Ours was in the middle of it. Rotation spotted west of town, near the old drive-in. Moving northeast at thirty-five miles an hour.

“That’s out by the cemetery,” I said.

Mother’s hand stilled on the napkin.

No one said anything. We all pictured the fresh dirt, the tent likely collapsed already, the flowers bent flat, Danny lying under the storm as if the weather had been waiting to finish the service.

Then my mother laughed.

It was not a happy sound, but it was alive.

“He would hate this,” she said. “All that money for flowers, and now they’re halfway to Iowa.”

I laughed too, once, and then it broke open into something uglier. I covered my face with both hands. I had not cried on the plane, or in the rental car, or when I passed the Dairy Queen where Danny and I used to count change for a shared Blizzard, pretending it was enough for two. But in the church basement, with the tornado coming and my brother already gone, my knees gave out.

Mother did not hug me right away. That also seemed fair.

Instead she reached across the table and pushed the cake toward me. The frosting had stained everyone’s teeth blue at a thousand birthdays, graduations, anniversaries held under fluorescent lights just like these.

“Eat,” she said.

“I’m not hungry.”

“Neither is he.”

So I took a plastic fork and cut into my brother’s name. The first bite was sugar and shortening and cardboard, the taste of every Midwestern condolence. Pastor Lyle turned up the radio. Children cried in the nursery room. Above us the wind found the building and shook it hard, rattling the basement windows in their wells.

Mother watched me chew.

“He kept your room the same,” she said. “Except he put his treadmill in there.”

“He never ran a day in his life.”

“Said he was going to start when you came home.”

The siren’s howl thinned under the roar outside. It sounded suddenly less like warning and more like mourning, like the whole town had leaned back its head and let out what it had been holding.

I thought of Danny at ten, daring me to stand in the ditch and face the summer wind. Danny at nineteen, carrying Dad’s boots in from the porch. Danny last month, leaving a message I deleted after seven seconds because I knew the shape of it already: his breath, his forgiveness, the terrible openness of his door.

The lights went out.

In the dark, my mother found my hand. Her fingers were cold and dry and stronger than I remembered.

“Stay down,” Pastor Lyle said, though none of us had moved.

The church groaned. Something enormous passed over us—not touching down, maybe, or touching down everywhere. The windows filled with dirt. The air smelled of rain, roots, splintered wood.

I held on to my mother’s hand and listened as the town where I had been born tried to leave the ground.

For one impossible second, I imagined Danny above us, laughing in that bright, reckless way, chasing the folding chairs across the cemetery, catching every ruined flower before it could vanish.

Then the roar moved east.

The radio kept talking. The children quieted. Water dripped somewhere steadily, counting what was left.

When the emergency lights flickered on, my mother’s face appeared red and shadowed, older by years or maybe only properly seen. She looked at our joined hands as if surprised to find them there.

“You’ll come to the grave tomorrow,” she said.

It was not a question.

“Yes,” I said.

Outside, the siren wound down, uncertainly, like a thing ashamed of all it had not been able to prevent.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense, lyrical paragraph blending grief, funeral food, weather radar, and tornado sirens, with the phrase “ground truth” used as a metaphor.
counterfactuals.output: The casseroles arrived warm as rumors, foil-lidded and sweating on the church basement tables while the weather radar bloomed green and yellow over the county like a bruise learning its colors, and all afternoon the tornado sirens kept lifting their mechanical throats above the hymns, above the clink of plastic forks in potato salad, above my aunt whispering that grief comes in bands, hook-shaped and rotating, impossible to name until it is already touching down. We stood there in our black clothes under fluorescent light, eating ham rolls and lemon bars while the sky lowered itself window by window, and I thought of you beneath the red clay, the only ground truth left to us: not the screen’s bright violence, not the warning polygon, not the preacher’s careful weather of heaven, but the raw fact of your absence pressed into the earth, changing the pressure in every room.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a prose-poem style passage about a post-funeral gathering at a dead brother’s house during severe weather; make it atmospheric, elegiac, and ominous.
counterfactuals.output:
After the burial we returned to my brother’s house because there was nowhere else for the living to go. The storm had come down hard from the hills, blackening the road behind us, and all the cars in the drive shone with rain like animals huddled against a fence. Inside, the rooms were lit too brightly. Coats steamed on chair backs. Someone had brought ham, someone had brought pie, someone had brought the old helpless sentences and set them out beside the paper plates.

The house kept making his noises without him.

Pipes knocked in the walls. The refrigerator shuddered and stopped and began again. In the hallway, where his boots still leaned with mud in their seams, water ticked from the eaves into a metal pan, patient as a clock. Every few minutes thunder crossed over us, not overhead but through the house, as if the sky had found the rafters and meant to take them apart.

We spoke softly because the dead were upstairs in every room. In the mirror above the mantel, our faces gathered and faded, gathered and faded, all of us wearing the same borrowed expression. My mother sat beneath his hunting photograph and held a cup she did not drink from. My uncle laughed once at something no one had said, and the laugh fell flat into the carpet. Children were told not to run, then ran anyway, their small socks flashing at the edge of grief like minnows in dark water.

Outside, the sycamores bent and turned their pale limbs to the windows. The creek behind the house, thin all summer, had swollen brown and muscular, dragging branches, dragging a child’s red ball, dragging some torn piece of the hillside down toward the culvert. We watched it as if it had news of him. We watched it rise by inches.

On the kitchen counter, covered dishes waited to be uncovered. Beneath the foil, casseroles breathed their warm onion breath. The women moved from sink to stove with the ancient competence of mourners, washing what was clean, folding what had already been folded, making order in the one place order would still consent to be made. In the next room, the men stood with their hands in their pockets and looked toward the windows whenever lightning whitened the glass.

His chair remained empty in the corner, not ceremonially, not on purpose, but with the terrible authority of absence. No one sat there. No one had to say why.

By evening the power flickered. The lamps dimmed and swelled. For one long second every bulb in the house went blue, and all our shadows rose behind us, tall and startled, as if called by name. Then the lights steadied, and the rain struck harder, fist after fist on the roof.

It seemed then that the house had become a boat, unmoored and crowded, carrying us through a country of water and wind, past the drowned fields, past the black pasture fence, past the grave fresh under its wreaths. My brother was not in the ground and not in the house, not in the stories we told badly, not in the shirt hanging behind his bedroom door. Yet everything leaned toward him. The storm leaned. The creek leaned. The old floorboards leaned under our feet.

And somewhere beyond the windows, beyond the yard where the porch light trembled in the rain, something vast and unfinished moved closer, wearing the weather for a face.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write in the style of contemporary literary fiction: mourners after a funeral, church ladies bringing casseroles, a muted TV showing a tornado warning, and the narrator reflecting on absence and uncertainty.
counterfactuals.output:
By four o’clock, the house had filled with food and weather.

The church ladies came in twos and threes, bearing their covered dishes as if each one contained a small, negotiated mercy. Hash brown casserole with its buttered crust. Green beans collapsed in mushroom soup. Ham biscuits wrapped in foil, still warm at the center. Someone had made banana pudding in a glass bowl, vanilla wafers softening into a kind of surrender. They moved through the kitchen with practiced grief, opening drawers they had no right to know and somehow knew anyway, finding serving spoons, tape, a marker for labeling lids.

On the television in the den, the sound was off. A red polygon shivered over the county map. The meteorologist’s mouth opened and closed around words we could not hear. Behind him, the radar bloomed green, yellow, violent pink. Every few minutes the screen cut to the same footage of a lowering sky over a field, the horizon bruised and strange.

No one turned up the volume. It seemed understood that there was already enough to listen for: ice knocking in plastic cups, the murmur of condolences, the back door sighing open and shut, the occasional sharp laugh from someone who did not mean to laugh and then looked ashamed.

My uncle sat in the recliner that had been my father’s and held a paper plate on his knees. He had taken a serving of everything and eaten none of it. Across the room, women from the choir arranged themselves on the sofa, their black dresses lifting slightly at the hems when the air conditioner came on. They spoke of the service, the flowers, the cemetery road gone soft from last night’s rain. They spoke around my mother, who sat upright in a straight-backed chair as if posture could keep something from spilling out of her.

People kept telling me he was at peace. They said this with the gentle insistence of those who need the sentence to be true for reasons of their own. I nodded. I accepted their hands, their damp eyes, the brief weight of their arms. But peace felt too final a word, too furnished. What I felt was absence, which had no furniture, no walls, no weather of its own. It was not an emptiness exactly. It was more like standing in a room where the music has stopped and realizing the silence had been there underneath it all along.

Outside, the sky lowered. The maple leaves turned their pale undersides to the wind. In the yard, the folding chairs from the reception tent trembled in uneven rows, as if a congregation had just risen from them and vanished.

I kept expecting my father to come in through the side door with rain on his shoulders, irritated by all the cars in the drive. He would ask why the television was muted. He would lift the foil from every dish, make a small approving noise over the macaroni, say somebody ought to bring those chairs in before the storm got them.

Instead, his boots remained by the mat, dark with old mud. His cap hung from its hook. The mail he had meant to open sat in a stack beside the phone.

The warning banner crawled silently across the bottom of the screen. TAKE SHELTER NOW. The words passed under footage of a town not yet struck, streets shining, trees bending in one direction. Everyone in the den watched without admitting they were watching. We were people who had gathered after one disaster and found another arriving on its own timetable, indifferent to ham, hymns, paperwork, the good silver set out for guests.

In the kitchen, someone asked where we kept the plastic wrap.

For a moment no one answered. Then my mother said, “Third drawer,” though she did not turn her head.

I thought of how much of a life is stored in such knowing. Third drawer. Top shelf. The key under the flowerpot. The pills with breakfast. The road that floods first. The sound a person makes clearing his throat in the dark.

And then, after, how knowledge becomes useless and sacred at the same time.

The lights flickered once. All conversation stopped, lifted its face. In that brief dimming, the windows went black and reflective, and I saw us there: the living assembled among the casseroles, holding plates, holding cups, holding on to whatever object had found its way into our hands. Behind our reflections, the storm gathered itself invisibly.

Then the power steadied. Someone exhaled. Someone said, “Lord.”

On the television, the red shape widened and moved east. I watched it cross the map toward us, or away from us; with the sound off it was impossible to tell.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a single-paragraph scene where a sibling’s cremation, a crowded funeral reception, and a possible tornado converge, emphasizing sensory detail and emotional restraint.
counterfactuals.output: The urn was heavier than it looked, warm only because I had been holding it too long, its brushed metal slick beneath my thumb while people pressed in around the church basement tables with paper plates of ham, potato salad, sweating cubes of cheese, their voices rising and folding back whenever the lights flickered. Someone had set my brother’s photograph between two grocery-store lilies, and the lilies gave off a sugary rot that mixed with coffee, wet wool, and the faint mineral smell of rain pushing through the open door upstairs. Aunt Carol kept asking if I wanted to sit, if I’d eaten, if the crematorium had “been kind,” and I nodded at each question as though they were all the same, watching the windows go the color of old coins. Outside, the siren began—not steady, not quite certain—then stopped, then started again, and the room paused just long enough for forks to hover and children to turn their faces toward the ceiling. In that brief quiet I could hear the ice machine drop a load into its bin, the soft scrape of my mother’s chair, the wind testing the building’s seams. “Probably just a warning,” someone said, and everyone resumed in smaller voices, closer together, while I kept both hands around the urn and felt, absurdly, that if the roof lifted away I should be ready not to spill him.
